title: Combining serology with case-detection, to allow the easing of restrictions against SARS-CoV-2: a modelling-based study in India
abstract: India's lockdown and subsequent restrictions against SARS-CoV-2, if lifted without any other mitigations in place, could risk a second wave of infection. A test-and-isolate strategy, using PCR diagnostic tests, could help to minimise the impact of this second wave. Meanwhile, population-level serological surveillance can provide valuable insights into the level of immunity in the population. Using a mathematical model, consistent with an Indian megacity, we examined how seroprevalence data could guide a test-and-isolate strategy, for fully lifting restrictions. For example, if seroprevalence is 20% of the population, we show that a testing strategy needs to identify symptomatic cases within 5-8 days of symptom onset, in order to prevent a resurgent wave from overwhelming hospital capacity in the city. This estimate is robust to uncertainty in the effectiveness of the lockdown, as well as in immune protection against reinfection. To set these results in their economic context, we estimate that the weekly cost of such a PCR-based testing programme would be less than 2.1% of the weekly economic loss due to the lockdown. Our results illustrate how PCR-based testing and serological surveillance can be combined to design evidence-based policies, for lifting lockdowns in Indian cities and elsewhere.

summary.oneLiner: A modelling study finds that pairing serosurveys with PCR test-and-isolate can let an Indian megacity lift lockdown without overwhelming hospitals, if testing is fast enough.
summary.overview: India's lockdown could trigger a second wave if lifted with no other measures. The authors built a compartmental model of an Indian megacity and tested two-pronged strategies: PCR testing to isolate symptomatic cases quickly, combined with serological (antibody) surveys to track population immunity. They find that at 20% seroprevalence, symptomatic cases must be isolated within roughly 5–8 days of symptom onset to keep a resurgent wave from overwhelming hospital capacity. They also estimate that such a testing programme would cost less than 2.1% of the weekly economic loss from the lockdown, though these are upper-bound, indicative figures. The results are illustrative and depend on many assumed parameters.
summary.question: How can seroprevalence data guide a test-and-isolate strategy so that restrictions on SARS-CoV-2 can be fully lifted in an Indian megacity without overwhelming hospital capacity, and how does the cost of such testing compare with the economic loss from lockdown?
summary.method: A deterministic compartmental mathematical model of SARS-CoV-2 transmission, stratified into three age groups, with waning immunity and reinfection. The authors simulated lockdown release with no other measures and with an intensive two-pronged programme (RT-PCR testing to isolate symptomatic cases, plus serosurveillance). They ran wide-uncertainty sampling over lockdown effectiveness and timing, asymptomatic transmission, and immunity, and sensitivity analyses for R0. Economic loss was estimated from sectoral productivity loss, and testing cost from an activity-based costing approach.
summary.data: No empirical patient or population dataset is used. The setting is a hypothetical megacity akin to Delhi, with model parameters drawn from assumptions and previous analyses. Economic estimates use sectoral composition of Delhi and per-test cost assumptions. The time period is the early COVID-19 period (paper received May 2020, accepted December 2020).
findings: At 20% seroprevalence at the point of lifting the lockdown, symptomatic cases need to be identified and isolated within 5–8 days of symptom onset to prevent a resurgent epidemic from overwhelming hospital capacity (for R0 = 2.5).

The required testing speed depends on R0: at R0 = 3 and 20% seroprevalence, symptomatic testing would need to identify cases within 2.5–4 days; including identification of half of asymptomatic infections relaxes this to 7–8 days.
The results are reported as robust to uncertainty in lockdown effectiveness and in immune protection against reinfection.

The weekly cost of a symptom-based PCR testing programme (an upper-bound scenario) is estimated at $26.68–42.12 million, which the authors say is less than 2.1% of the weekly economic loss due to lockdown.
The productivity loss from lockdown is estimated at 58–83.4%, equivalent to an economic loss of $1372–$1979 million per week.
The authors note that the economic estimate captures only productivity loss and likely understates the long-run loss from demand-side effects.

Serosurveillance is described as potentially valuable for informing the intensity of testing needed, though the authors note antibody test accuracy issues at the individual level and only consider population-level use.
summary.whyItMatters: For policymakers in Indian cities and elsewhere, the paper suggests serosurveys can guide how intensive test-and-isolate programmes must be before restrictions are lifted. The authors argue the testing cost appears small relative to lockdown losses, which they present as supporting evidence-based decisions about easing restrictions. They caution that the cost figures are indicative upper bounds and that the model is illustrative rather than a precise forecast.
